image_description: A low-angle, close-up view of a massive radio telescope dish against a clear blue sky. The image highlights the intricate steel lattice support structure (truss work) behind a semi-transparent or mesh reflective surface. The parabolic curvature is evident from the perspective distortion of the grid lines converging toward the center. A central hub/feed assembly is visible at the bottom center, though the specific feed horn is obscured by the angle.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Enormous parabolic dish antenna of colossal scale, dwarfing all surrounding structures.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The framing and perspective clearly indicate a structure of massive scale. The curvature of the horizon-like rim at the top confirms the parabolic shape.
The grid lines of the support structure follow a consistent, smooth mathematical curve characteristic of a parabola. No warping or irregularities are visible.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Massive installation spanning an area visible from great distances.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image is a tight crop looking up at the dish; the surrounding landscape or full footprint is not visible to verify the 'area visible from great distances' claim.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Receiver feed horn at focal point of dish.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The camera angle is from below/inside the dish looking up. The focal point would be suspended in front of the dish (above the camera's view) or obscured by the central hub structure visible at the bottom. It is not directly visible.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Alt-azimuth or equatorial mount for celestial tracking.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The mounting mechanism is located on the exterior/back of the dish and is completely occluded by the dish itself in this view.
While the structure exists, its ability to rotate cannot be verified from a static image, and the mechanical bearings are not visible.
The foundation is at ground level, which is outside the frame of this upward-looking shot.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Metal mesh or solid aluminum panel dish surface.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image clearly shows a metal mesh/grid construction supported by a steel truss lattice, consistent with radio telescope design.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Astronomical instrument for detecting radio-frequency emissions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visual features (large parabolic mesh dish) are unique to radio telescopes, confirming its identity as such an instrument.
Same as the alt-azimuth mount checkpoint; the mechanism is occluded.

selected_experts.reason: To confirm the specific class label and distinguish it from similar structures like satellite dishes or solar concentrators.
To verify the consistency of the parabolic curvature and ensure the complex lattice structure does not exhibit 'melting' or depth ordering errors common in AI generation.
To check for broken connections or fused bars in the complex truss work, ensuring structural integrity.
To detect any subtle texture anomalies or noise patterns in the sky or metal surfaces.

focus_areas: Consistency of the parabolic grid geometry
Structural integrity of the steel truss intersections
Texture realism of the metal mesh vs. sky background
custom_prompts_for_reflector: Pay close attention to the intersection points of the steel lattice. In AI-generated images, these often blur or fuse incorrectly. Verify if the perspective distortion of the grid remains mathematically consistent across the entire dish surface.
